before: With nullable analysis enabled, string? says a reference may be null. string expresses an intended non-null reference. The compiler uses these annotations for warnings; it does not add a runtime null guard automatically.
A null check narrows the possible state. Inside name != null, accessing name.Length is safe for this local variable. The else branch handles the missing value.
The null-forgiving ! operator only suppresses a warning; it does not turn null into an object. Prefer checking or supplying a real fallback. #nullable enable turns the analysis on for the file.
Expected behavior from this example: Missing. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer task: Use an empty string, then null. Explain why a missing value and a zero-length string take different paths. Use a .NET 10 console project with C# 14; reading completion does not verify this local work.
after: Nullable-reference analysis lets the compiler warn when code may use a missing object. #nullable enable turns these checks on for this file.
string? says a text reference may be null. string expresses the intent that it is not null. These marks help the compiler; they do not automatically insert checks when the program runs.
name != null checks that a value exists. Inside that branch, this local variable is safe to use. The else branch handles missing text.
The program prints Missing. name is null, so the condition is false and the else branch runs.
Putting ! after a value can silence a nullable warning. It does not create a missing object or prevent a null error. Use a real check or backup value when the value may be absent.
